Ana, I could not join yesterday. Give me the short version — where are we?
Two things. First, the document. The new draft states that the term is three years, and it requires ninety days notice before renewal.
Ninety days? That is longer than before.
It is. And second, the people. Their lawyer said they wanted the longer term, and he told me they could accept sixty days if we moved on the penalty.
No. That is why I am separating the two. The draft still says ninety. Sixty was something they said on a call, with a condition. It is not in the wording yet.
Understood. That distinction is exactly what I needed. Send me the two lines in writing and I will take it from here.
He said they could accept sixty days, if we moved on the penalty.
That is not in the wording yet.
Let me separate what the document says from what they said.

Here is something nobody teaches young lawyers, and it costs them years. When you are on a call and you want to talk about a clause, do not read the clause out loud. Please do not. The people on that call have the document in front of them and they cannot follow legal drafting by ear anyway. What you do instead is you report it. You say: clause five requires us to give thirty days notice. Or: the agreement states that the term renews automatically unless one party objects. One short sentence, in your own words, with a reporting verb at the front. States, requires, provides, sets out, specifies. That is the whole trick. And when you are reporting what a person said, not what a document says, remember the tense moves back. He said the deadline was Friday. Not is. Was. Small thing, but in a negotiation summary that small thing decides whether people think the deadline is still open.

I want to tell you about a mistake that cost my company a lot of money, because it was a language mistake, not a legal one. We were closing a deal and our lawyer sent a summary of the call. She wrote that the counterparty said they can extend the deadline. Can. Present tense. Everyone on my side read that and understood that the extension was agreed. It was not. What they had actually said, three weeks earlier, was that they could extend it, if we paid the difference. She had reported their words without moving the tense back, and without the condition. So we planned everything around a deadline that did not exist. Nobody lied. One verb, one missing condition, and a whole project moved. Now I read every summary twice, and I always ask the same question. Is this what the document says, or is this what somebody said?
